scope: Tracking project issues and defects from report to close: identifying and triaging new issues, assessing severity apart from priority, severity scales, owning each issue, tracking status to resolution, escalating critical and long-unresolved issues, recording how an issue was resolved and linking the fix, duplicates and not-planned closes, and the issue log as history. Covers the project-management bodies (PMBOK via a public secondary, ISO 21502, PRINCE2 7, the Scrum Guide, the Kanban Guide, ITIL 4 via a public secondary) and the trackers GitHub, Jira, Linear, Bugzilla and Google Issue Tracker. Production incidents are cookbook/guidelines/shipping/incident-response's, security vulnerability triage is cookbook/guidelines/reviewing/security/vulnerability-prioritization's, risks are risk-tracking's and the linking convention is project-record-linking's.
research_type: How-to / troubleshooting (intent Do; domain issue triage and resolution; Product/how-to LOW-MEDIUM bar, broad independent consensus)

questions.text: Best practices: what is current best practice for this topic?
Known solutions: what solutions, patterns, libraries and tools already exist, and how do they compare?
Platform guidelines: what do the platform owners' own guidelines say, for each platform the topic touches (Apple, Android, Windows, web, the databases and runtimes concerned)?
The expert's view: if we hired an expert consultant in this topic, what would they tell us: what to do, what to avoid, and what people usually get wrong?

methodology.method: guidelines/researching/process/research-methodology-and-sources: orient, go to authoritative sources (the project-management bodies' own texts or their owners' public summaries, the tracker vendors' documentation for their own products, large open-source projects' published triage policies), chain citations, corroborate across independent publishers, record provenance at generation time.
methodology.search_strategy: WebSearch for triage policy, severity and priority definitions, resolution fields, closing keywords, escalation and issue-log guidance; every cited page fetched (curl converted with textutil, WebFetch where curl was blocked, pdftotext for the CDC newsletter PDF, the Kubernetes guide fetched raw from GitHub, the IEEE TSE abstract read from OpenAlex) and each quote re-checked against the fetched text. Searches named the topic only.
methodology.inclusion: Primary sources first: tracker vendors' docs for their own products (GitHub, Atlassian Jira and Jira Service Management, Linear, Google Issue Tracker), Mozilla's and Kubernetes' and Chromium's published triage policies, the Scrum Guide, the Kanban Guide, PeopleCert's PRINCE2 7 article by a PRINCE2 7 co-author, a U.S. CDC project-management newsletter quoting PMBOK. Expert sources (Spolsky; a peer-reviewed IEEE TSE study) for the expert's-view question.
methodology.exclusion: Search-result snippets, vendor SEO blogs and listicles (Plane, Inflectra, DEV Community, bug0), pages that could not be fetched (PMI library 403, GitLab handbook behind auth, a finance-ni.gov.uk 404, the Open University and UCL repository pages 403), and any quote not found in the fetched page.
methodology.scoring: guidelines/researching/evidence/verification-and-trust-scoring: Authority 30 + Independent corroboration 25 + Accuracy 20 + Currency 10 + Transparency 15, capped by the Product/how-to LOW-MEDIUM domain bar (broad independent consensus among practitioners' and vendors' current documentation).

summary: Five of the seven rules hold at SHOULD strength: triage with a severity assessment (Mozilla, Kubernetes, Chromium, Atlassian, Linear), tracking status to resolution (Jira, Google Issue Tracker, Linear, Atlassian; the Scrum and Kanban guides on actively removing impediments), escalating critical issues (Mozilla S1 full attention and Release Management notice, Kubernetes critical-urgent, Chromium and Google P0), a critical issue having an owner or being escalated, and a resolved issue referencing what resolved it (Jira resolutions, GitHub state_reason and closing keywords, the CDC issue log). 'Every issue has severity and status' is contradicted as worded: Mozilla exempts tasks and enhancements from severity, and GitHub, Jira and Linear ship no severity field at all; status holds for every issue, severity for defects. 'Link issues to specialist findings' is unsupported: no source has specialist findings; sources support only linking related records. The topic misses: severity kept apart from priority, a defined severity scale, rationale for severity changes, severity set by the assessor rather than the reporter (priority inflation), a documented escalation path, escalating issues unresolved past a time limit, a named triage owner or rotation, triage within a time bound, one owner per issue, a resolution reason from a fixed set, linking the fixing change, closing duplicates against the canonical issue, closing not-planned work definitively, verifying the fix before close, keeping closed issues as history, telling stakeholders how it was resolved, minimum issue fields, a small priority scale, one tracker everyone uses, issues covering more than defects, and flagging stale issues.
open_questions: Which severity scale the cookbook adopts: Mozilla's four levels (S1 Catastrophic to S4 Small/Trivial) or Atlassian's three (Critical, Major, Minor), or another.
Whether tasks and enhancements carry a severity, or only defects (Mozilla allows N/A for tasks and enhancements).

The escalation time limit for an unresolved critical issue, and who it escalates to (Mozilla assigns S1 within 2 business days and notifies Release Management; Linear's example is a 24 hour SLA for Urgent).
Whether the reporter (or a named verifier) must confirm a fix before the issue is closed, or the fixer may close it.
Whether the rule to link issues to specialist findings stays, since no source covers specialist findings; the general linking convention is project-record-linking's.
Whether priority stays optional beside severity (Mozilla makes it optional) or is required.
limitations: PMBOK is paywalled and PMI's library page returned 403; its issue definition and issue-log guidance are taken from a U.S. CDC project-management newsletter that quotes it.
ISO 21502 and ISO 31000 are paywalled; ISO's TC 258 page describes ISO 21502 only as high-level practice guidance and holds no public issue text, so no ISO claim is made.
ITIL 4 is paywalled and AXELOS has no public text on problem management; the known-error definition is taken from Atlassian's ITSM page, a secondary source with a commercial interest.
SAFe and LeSS were not researched; no claim rests on them.
The IEEE TSE priority-inflation paper's full text could not be fetched (repository pages returned 403); only its abstract, read from OpenAlex, is quoted, and its metric results are not used.

Production incidents (cookbook/guidelines/shipping/incident-response) and security vulnerability triage (cookbook/guidelines/reviewing/security/vulnerability-prioritization) are excluded as those topics' subjects.
The CDC newsletter PDF is two-column; its quotes were reassembled across line breaks from pdftotext output.
No source gives a measured effect size for any triage practice; every finding here is practice consensus, not a statistical result.
license: MIT (this research record); quoted material remains under its sources' terms and is quoted for verification.

trust.basis: GitHub's own current docs; one publisher; the absence of a severity label is read from the default-label list.

claims.question: experts-view
claims.claim: A good team keeps all issues in one tracker that everyone uses; if filing is too much work, people go around it.
claims.query: Painless bug tracking database of bugs hallmark
claims.quote: Keeping a database of bugs is one of the hallmarks of a good software team. | For the bug database to work, everybody needs to use it, and if entering bugs “formally” is too much work, people will go around the bug database.

trust.basis: Widely cited expert article; old but about stable human behaviour; one publisher.

claims.question: experts-view
claims.claim: An expert holds that a good bug report needs exactly three things (steps to reproduce, what was expected, what was seen) and no more.
claims.query: Painless bug tracking every good bug report needs exactly three things
claims.quote: Every good bug report needs exactly three things.

trust.basis: One expert article, old; the three items are listed on the page after this sentence. Second check 2026-11-24: refuted (quote-found yes, supports-claim partly): The quote says only that a good report needs "exactly three things" and does not name them. The page names them in the next sentence ("Steps to reproduce, What you expected to see, and What you saw instead"), so a longer quote would support the claim; lowered 50->30.

claims.question: experts-view
claims.claim: Keep the tracker's fields and priority levels few: extra fields and finer priorities make issues harder to file and rank, for little return.
claims.query: avoid the temptation to add new fields to the bug database; Linear no custom priorities
claims.quote: Avoid the temptation to add new fields to the bug database. | Adding too many options makes it harder to set priority and leads to diminishing returns.

trust.basis: An expert and a vendor independently say the same; no measured effect.

claims.question: experts-view
claims.claim: People filing issues inflate their priority, and a separate triage team does not cure it; severity is set by those who assess the issue, not by the reporter.
claims.query: priority inflation bug repair assessor; Bugzilla severity should not be set by people filing bugs
claims.quote: Priority inflation occurs when a Quality-Assurance (QA) engineer or a project manager requesting a feature inflates the priority of their task so that developers deliver the fix or the new functionality more quickly. We survey developers and show that priority inflation occurs and misallocates developer time. | We then show that the common mitigation strategy of having a bug triage team assigning priorities does not resolve priority inflation and slows development. | It should not be set by people filing bugs.

citations.title: The Assessor's Dilemma: Improving Bug Repair via Empirical Game Theory
citations.author: Carlos Gavidia-Calderon, Federica Sarro, Mark Harman and Earl T. Barr
citations.publisher: IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering (abstract via OpenAlex)

trust.basis: Peer-reviewed study (abstract only; its metrics not used) independently matched by Mozilla's rule that reporters do not set severity.

claims.question: experts-view
claims.claim: Important issues get re-filed, often as duplicates, so triage expects and merges them.
claims.query: Chromium triage best practices duplicate re-file important issues
claims.quote: People will re-file (and often duplicate) important issues.

trust.basis: One publisher's practitioner guidance; not corroborated. Second check 2026-11-24: refuted (quote-found yes, supports-claim partly): Chromium uses this line to justify spending triage time on recent issues and letting old ones go. Its point is that important problems resurface as new reports. It does not say triage should expect duplicates and merge them, beyond noting that old issues often "have not been properly duped"; lowered 50->30.
